title: Count Fertile Pyramids in a Land
summary: A farmer owns a rectangular grid of land with m rows and n columns, where each cell is either fertile (1) or barren (0).
statement: A farmer owns a rectangular grid of land with m rows and n columns, where each cell is either fertile (1) or barren (0). The task is to count the total number of pyramidal and inverse pyramidal plots of land that meet specific criteria. A pyramidal plot has an apex at the top and covers cells in a triangular shape, while an inverse pyramidal plot has an apex at the bottom and also covers cells in a triangular shape. Each plot must consist of more than one fertile cell. The grid's boundary cells are considered barren. The goal is to identify and count all such valid plots within the given grid.
constraints: grid is a nonempty rectangular binary matrix.
A pyramid has a fertile apex and successively wider fully fertile rows; an inverse pyramid points upward.
Count both orientations with height at least two.
hints: For each apex, only the minimum supported height among the three cells in the next row can extend it.
Run one DP bottom-up for downward pyramids and one top-down for inverse pyramids.
dp=1+min(three supporting neighbors); add dp-1 at each fertile cell.
A height h pyramid exists exactly when all three supporting subpyramids reach height h-1, and dp-1 counts every permitted height at that apex.
editorial: A height h pyramid exists exactly when all three supporting subpyramids reach height h-1, and dp-1 counts every permitted height at that apex.

tests.explanation: There is one downward and one upward height-two pyramid.
The full 3-by-3 grid contains four height-two and two additional nested pyramids.
